text: Every Pod gets a brand-new IP address each time it's replaced — a rolling update, a crash, a reschedule — and that address is gone for good. Nothing that depends on a Pod's own IP can survive that. A Service is Kubernetes's answer: one stable virtual IP and DNS name sitting in front of a changing set of Pods. This lesson covers the three Service types you'll actually use — ClusterIP, NodePort, and LoadBalancer — and each one is a strict superset of the one before it.

Think of these three as a ladder, not three unrelated options. ClusterIP is the foundation: a virtual IP reachable only inside the cluster, found by a selector that matches Pod labels, not Pod names. NodePort takes everything ClusterIP does and adds one more thing — the same fixed port, opened on every node. LoadBalancer takes everything NodePort does and adds a real external load balancer, provisioned by your cloud provider, pointed at that NodePort. Each step up is additive, never a replacement.

Here's a ClusterIP Service in real YAML. The selector, app: payments-api, is a label query — Kubernetes keeps the list of healthy endpoints behind this Service current as matching Pods come and go, with zero changes to the Service object across a rolling update. port 80 is what callers send traffic to on the Service's virtual IP; targetPort 8080 is the actual port the container listens on inside the Pod. Since ClusterIP is the default, this type field could even be left out.

Add type: NodePort and one field, nodePort: 30080, and this Service is now reachable at that port on every node's IP. It doesn't matter which node actually has a matching Pod, because kube-proxy forwards the request to wherever that Pod really lives. NodePort is mostly a building block: useful for quick testing against a live cluster, useful on-prem where there's no cloud load balancer, and it's exactly the foundation LoadBalancer builds on next.

Change type to LoadBalancer, and Kubernetes asks your cloud provider's controller to stand up a real external load balancer — an Azure Load Balancer, an AWS NLB, a GCP load balancer — pointed at the NodePort running on every node. Run kubectl get svc right after creating this, and EXTERNAL-IP reads pending for a short while before a real public IP appears, your signal that the Service is now reachable from the open internet.

One LoadBalancer Service generally means one cloud load balancer, billed and managed separately — expensive once you have more than a couple of externally facing apps. Next lesson picks up exactly there: Ingress, which puts many HTTP and HTTPS routes behind a single shared entry point instead of one load balancer per Service.
